newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dollar posts another steady day.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dollar posts another steady day.

text.p: The Australian dollar remained range-bound and showing no inclination to make a near term break after another day of unremarkable trading, dealers said.

While the pushing back of expectations of a rate cut after the Reserve Bank of Australian (RBA) bulletin was released on Wednesday supported the Australian dollar, Asian selling interest was capping its topside, they said.
By 4.45 p.m. (0645 GMT), the Australian dollar was at US$0.7915/20 up from an early US$0.7913/18 and a Wednesday close of US$0.7910/15. During the day, it reached a high of US$0.7924.

"The Aussie got a little bit of boost from the reports on the front pages of newspapers saying the RBA was thinking about not cutting again because of wages, but there's a lot of selling interest above US$0.7920/25," one trader said.

While the dollar has held to a US$0.7855-0.7965 range over the past month, more recently it has been held to a narrower US$0.7880-0.7930 band. Despite this, there has been good two way trade, especially when the market approaches the extremities.
Traders said there was talk of samurai-related buying today, but the yen cross appeared toppish at around 89 yen, and it was Asian sellers who were prepared to sell into the rallies.
Conversely, there were also rumours, which appeared on Wednesday, that a large buy order had been placed at US$0.7880/85, which was supporting the unit on dips.
"It looks like there's some sort of strangle out there, although no one really knows," the trader said.
The Australian dollar ended at 88.60/70 yen, having weakened in late trade as the U.S. dollar fell under 112 yen, from an early 88.82/92 and a Wednesday close of 88.76/86.
In trade weighted terms, the dollar finished at 58.6, level with its previous close, but down on its opening 58.7.

While Wednesday's RBA Bulletin dented hopes of a rate cut in 1996, the market had not ruled out a cut completely, in part because when the RBA last cut rates on July 31, it came about two weeks after the RBA had warned about the dangers of a wages blowout in their last quarterly bulletin, traders said.
In its quarterly report on the economy, the RBA said that based on current projections, and given their concerns over wages growth, a cut now could store up problems for the future.
The market had widely expected a 50 basis point cut in rates from the current 7.0 percent level would be announced in early November, following next week's key inflation and wages data.

"The kneejerk reaction was to buy Aussie on the back of that, but I think the market's got in and thought about it, some of the economists have thought about it as well, and come to the conclusion that if wages don't blow out they can still ease again, so we're back in that thought pattern," the trader said.
In the bulletin, the RBA did not rule out an interest rate cut, saying weaker than expected growth and a reduction in inflationary expectations would support the case for a cut.

Those looking for a cut took comfort from the fact the report was written before the release of weak September labour force data and the National Australia Bank quarterly business survey showing continued softness in business conditions.
Next week's third quarter wages and inflation data are also expected to come in at levels supportive of a rate cut, economists said.
The key local event on Friday is the release of September merchandise imports data. Economists surveyed by Reuters expect a 1.0 percent rise, following a 1.1 percent rise in August.
